title: Leopard Bites on Ancient Jawbone Show Humans Were Once Prey
summary: Nearly 2 million years ago, a leopard in Africa sank its teeth into the face of an early human. The bite left tiny tooth marks on the person's jawbone. That bone, now analyzed by scientists, tells a chilling story: humans were once prey. The fossil belongs to Homo habilis, one of the earliest members of our genus. It was found at Olduvai Gorge in Tanzania, a site that has yielded many ancient human bones since the 1930s. At first glance, the marks on the jawbone looked like scratches. But a recent study used artificial intelligence (AI) to analyze them. The team, led by Marina Vegara-Riquelme of the University of Alcalá in Spain, trained AI on thousands of tooth-mark images from modern carnivores. Different predators have different eating habits: hyenas often scavenge dead carcasses, while leopards rarely eat meat they didn't kill. Knowing which animal left the marks would reveal whether the Homo habilis was hunted or died another way. "Two Homo habilis specimens show tooth marks most likely inflicted by leopards," Vegara-Riquelme said. That suggests the early human was hunted, not scavenged. "That individual was preyed upon," said study co-author Manuel Domínguez-Rodrigo. "Not scavenged." This discovery helps solve a fossil mystery and raises questions about a time when humans held a precarious spot in the food web. Sometimes they ate meat; other times, they were the meat being eaten. For millions of years before Homo habilis, our ape ancestors spent most of their time in trees, escaping danger by climbing. But by the time Homo habilis evolved, humans walked upright and spent far more time on the ground — where lions and leopards lived. To survive, they likely relied on each other for protection, living in groups, sharing information about dangers, and teaching each other skills. Over generations, these behaviors could have helped humans become more cooperative and successful. Today, it's easy to imagine our early ancestors as fearless hunters. But before we became one of the world's most successful predators, we first had to survive life as prey.
why_it_matters: The finding reframes the story of human origins: cooperation, group living and information sharing may have developed less as hunting tactics than as survival tactics against predators. It also shows how new tools such as machine learning are letting scientists squeeze fresh evidence out of fossils collected decades ago.

background_read: Olduvai Gorge (a deep, dry canyon in northern Tanzania, in East Africa) is one of the most famous fossil sites on Earth. From the 1930s onwards, archaeologists Louis and Mary Leakey — a husband-and-wife team whose excavations there reshaped the study of human origins — recovered hundreds of early human bones and stone tools from its layers of sediment.

Homo habilis is an early member of our genus, Homo, that lived in Africa around two million years ago, close in time to the bite marks described here. Compared with modern humans it had a smaller brain and a shorter body, and it was among the first of our relatives to make and use simple stone tools — which is one reason its fossils are studied so closely.

The University of Alcalá (a public university in Spain, near Madrid) led the new study. The researchers applied machine learning — computer programs that find patterns in large sets of examples — to tooth marks, a method increasingly used in archaeology because it can separate marks that look almost identical to the human eye. Today the idea of humans as prey sounds strange, but palaeontologists (scientists who study fossils) have long argued that early hominins were a normal part of the menu for big African carnivores such as leopards, hyenas and sabre-toothed cats.

perspectives.description: The study shows AI can identify the predator behind marks that look like ordinary scratches, opening museum collections to fresh analysis without digging up anything new. It also turns a single damaged jawbone into evidence about behaviour, not just anatomy.

Tooth-mark identification is genuinely difficult: bone can be scratched by roots, trampling, digging tools or weathering in ways that mimic teeth. The conclusion rests on two specimens and on AI trained with modern carnivores, so it is a strong likelihood rather than a certainty.

Becoming prey fits the long arc of human evolution: hominins left the trees for open ground while still small-bodied and slow, entering a food web already ruled by big cats and hyenas. Group living and shared alarm calls are common anti-predator strategies across many primates, so this may be an old inheritance rather than a new invention.

If AI can re-read old fossils, other collections may reveal how often early humans were eaten, and by which species. That could shift the classic image of early humans as fearless hunters toward a picture in which they were also prey — with consequences for how we explain the origins of cooperation and social learning.
